They Will Kill You ups the ante with absurdism, gore, and cinematic homages it wears proudly on its chest. It might not be the most nuanced action film of the year, but They Will Kill You makes up for it with style and wild abandon.
She Dances comes off as a tremendously powerful drama about family and loss that's built on the complexity of well-written characters without falling victim to tropes of the subgenre.

With Mike & Nick & Nick & Alice, Grabinski has taken the bones of a gangster movie and added laugh-out-loud humor, wild references, needle drops, and time travel, and blended them into one of the most fun films to come out in 2026.
Drag is a compelling 82 minutes, but even with that short runtime, it starts to feel like that concept is about to start running on fumes.

Pizza Movie not only feels like an homage to the films that came before it, the types of movies that you’d watch over and over again, catching and memorizing every little joke, but a solid new step forward in the stoner comedy canon.
The Sun Never Sets is a welcome return for Swanberg that shows he hasn’t missed a beat.
Goldman has a lot on his mind, but Sender sometimes feels like when you have too many ideas, and you try to say them all at once, but it comes out garbled and confusing.
The Saviors doesn’t have the nuance or the depth to explore its well-intentioned concept in any way other than in the most obvious, direct ways.

While Kill Me doesn’t stick its landing, this is an impressive debut from Peter Warren, and it shows how well he can mix extremely dark subject matter with an engaging mystery that’s also quite funny.
Byrk’s feature debut is silly and goofy as hell, but also surprisingly sweet in its approach to this group of fledgling jackasses.
It is abundantly clear that Tow was made with the purest of intentions, and it's not a bad movie by any means, but it doesn't have the emotional heft that it should have.
Brian isn’t just the best film out of this year’s SXSW — it’s one of the funniest films to come out this year so far.

Over Your Dead Body begins with a captivating premise centered on two playful actors pushing themselves and the roles we expect from them, only to be spoiled by a story that leans too far into the darkness.
Vampires of the Velvet Lounge is perhaps one of the most egregious examples of preemptively preparing for second-screen viewing.
Forbidden Fruits has the style and the look, but it lacks cohesion and focus; a film that doesn’t narratively hold together with a story that leaves far too much unanswered.
This isn’t going to be the next John Wick, but it's certainly an enjoyable, often unexpectedly grisly action film and a solid way to spend 90 minutes.
Wardriver feels familiar. It's Dane DeHaan that makes it worth investing in. If only they had gone deeper, Wardriver could have lifted itself past expectations into something more compelling.
Hokum doesn’t overcomplicate itself, but rather, it sticks to the classics: strange figures moving in the dark, claustrophobic scenarios, and the old trusty jump scare.

media_title: Paul McCartney: Man on the Run

Dead Deer High is a quiet, compassionate film that understands grief as something lived through, not neatly overcome.
An absolute must‑see, Kill Me offers a career‑defining best for Day while reaffirming Williams as a star. Come for the laughs, stay for the heart, and get pulled into the heady whodunnit.
Seekers of Infinite Love is a road‑trip movie filled with unexpected comedic detours and an emotional ending that drives home the enduring power of family.
Julian of Norwich and her work come to vivid life in filmmaker Caroline Golum’s sophomore feature, which boasts a highly stylized, homespun aesthetic that is guaranteed to charm you.

media_title: Ready or Not 2: Here I Come
rt_quote: With plenty of action set pieces, some fun loophole exploits, and a dynamite chemistry between Weaving and Newton, Ready Or Not 2 is that surprisingly satisfying sequel that acts as the proper DLC expansion you would hope for in a game you love.
Boots Riley reminds us that even though there is much to be angry about the world we live in, there is still hope that we can rally, strategize, and make it better.
Home Delivery is a comedy brave enough to sit with emotional messiness and find real heart.
At times, genius and at others, just cringey, The Musical the mean-spirited movie of the year.
Music can heal, but Matter of Time shows how it can also change lives by turning performance into purpose.

Extra Geography, is a brisk 94-minute drama that is unafraid to be both dryly funny and yet awkwardly discomforting at the same time. Viewers may find comparisons to Booksmart or The Holdovers appropriate, which in itself is high praise.
THX 1138 requires a lot of thinking and a vivid imagination. It’s not an easy movie.
This is Hannah Lynch’s film, who does an amazing job as our anchor to both reality and absurdity. Mum, I’m Alien Pregnant is exactly what it says it is, and yet also, much more.
A time capsule of a certain era of indie film experimentation, Nadja might lack the gloss of later vampire films with larger budgets, but that’s part of what makes it such a fun watch.
In any other year, it would be an important documentary; in 2025, it is essential.

media_title: Can She Bake a Cherry Pie?
rt_quote: A delightful and nostalgic glimpse into the past, Can She Bake a Cherry Pie? deserves a place in the pantheon of great New York City movies.
Dominik Sedlar’s Vindicta is a harrowing tale that is anchored by exquisite direction and a star-turning lead performance.
Zoe Eisenberg’s assured directorial debut swims in moral ambiguity, but it’s equally concerned with loneliness, inertia, and the quiet despair that can settle in when life feels suspended.

Maybe The Crooked Man will only appeal to hardcore Hellboy fans who want to see another adaptation of their favorite character, but it is also a very enjoyable riff on folk horror and The Evil Dead with some comic book flourishes.

Watching Godzilla ‘54 and having an absolute ball with it, I’m not surprised that 70 years later, Godzilla is still doing big box office numbers and wowing audiences. And I don’t think he has any plans of retiring in the near or distant future.
Perhaps in their haste to be the first ones out with a Winnie-the-Pooh movie, the filmmakers unfortunately skimped on the writing for the non-Pooh characters, leaving them lifeless and feeling fake.

media_title: Winnie the Pooh: Blood and Honey II
rt_quote: After watching Winnie-the-Pooh: Blood and Honey 2, I’m excited to see what these filmmakers have in store and how weird they’re going to go with this whole thing.
A wonderful addition to the MCU and the superhero canon, The Fantastic Four: First Steps is a breath of fresh air in the genre while also being unique in how much it enjoys being a superhero movie.

This is one of the best movies about movies I’ve seen in a long time. It is a love letter to the movie, the genre, and the filmmakers made with never-before-seen footage and fans who can see beneath the surface of the film.

We Bury the Dead is a rumination on grief and the way we lose loved ones sometimes without a goodbye or on bad terms. It is also a road trip movie, a haunted house horror, and a showcase for the talents of Daisy Ridley.
Just as in Zootopia, the world-building and neat details are incredible. Expanding into the reptile world and the swamps gives the filmmakers room to build upon the rich world of the original movie.
A Girl is a Gun is a defiantly quirky and incredibly entertaining example of what made Moullet the chaos agent of the French New Wave.
Little Trouble Girls takes a lovely, lyrical approach to time-worn tropes, the result of which is a film that entrances the audience despite its flaws.
Watching it fills me with sadness for what we lost when Swanson suddenly stopped production; nonetheless, some Queen Kelly is better than no Queen Kelly.

With the rich color and texture present in every frame of the film looking positively rejuvenated in 4K, there’s never been a better time for Four Nights of a Dreamer to finally take the prominent place it deserves in Bresson’s filmography.
Riefenstahl should be the last word on its subject—not just because it is the definitive one, but also because it is the last one we need. She doesn’t deserve any more.
In the end, Fuqua's Michael is a beautifully performed but carefully curated story. It celebrates more than it questions and remembers more than it reveals.

media_title: A Savage Art: The Life & Cartoons of Pat Oliphant
rt_quote: A Savage Art is both informative and inspiring. It reminds us that art can challenge power, provoke thought, and leave a lasting imprint on public life.
The nods to its influences can feel a little on-the-nose, but there's enough that's genuinely its own here.
The film's bold approach to structure, theme, and performance ensures it leaves a lasting impression.
It gestures towards profundity but never quite earns it.
You'll enjoy it while it's on, and Taylor-Johnson, Theo James et al are worth watching throughout. You just might not find yourself thinking about it much once it’s over.
Borgli has made something genuinely rare here: a relationship film with real teeth, one that refuses to let either its characters, or its audience, off the hook.
It may not redefine the genre, but it delivers a cheerful, imaginative escape that should keep family audiences thoroughly entertained.
They Will Kill You is messy, excessive, and uneven in places,  but if you're in the mood for something wild and unpretentious, it delivers exactly what it promises.
This is an impressively visually polished, heartfelt and musically engaging adaptation that brings a familiar story to life with sincerity and style.
While it does not fully realise its potential, the film succeeds in sparking conversation and challenging its audience.
Power Ballad has all the makings of a crowd-pleasing hit. From the opening frame to the end credits, the smile never left my face. Power Ballad might just be the feel-good hit of the year.

Boots Riley is a filmmaker with a true vision, one who understands how powerful the medium can be when used to say something meaningful. Here he takes big swings, delivering something that feels fresh, original, and unapologetically bold.
Overall, Standout is a heartfelt and accessible documentary that delivers an important message about embracing difference.
Dead Man’s Wire might not break new ground, but it’s a really solid thriller that knows what it’s doing.

media_title: Ready or Not 2: Here I Come
rt_quote: Here I Come is entertaining, well-acted, and occasionally reminds you why the concept works. But it never recaptures the lightning-in-a-bottle thrill of the original.
Project Hail Mary is a triumphant science fiction adventure. It manages to be smart without alienating those less au fait with the science, and heartfelt without falling into the overly sentimental.
Expect tension, surprises, and more than a little heartbreak.
As it is, it’s an intriguing but deeply flawed experiment, It is worth watching for the performances and audacity, even if it doesn’t make a lot of sense.
Wildly inventive, visually stunning, and laugh-out-loud hilarious, Hoppers is not just a return to form; it’s Pixar at full creative power. I cannot wait to watch it again and again.
The  franchise deserves better than this halfbacked attempt at a reboot. Plus, we actually liked Melissa Barrera, so just bring her back already.
A masterwork of modern political cinema, and one of the year’s most daring achievements.

media_title: Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die
rt_quote: Varbinski's message is clear - even if it's sometimes a little on too on the nose - AI offers the comfort of endless resets, curated realities and instant gratification. But while resistance might be futile, it remains our most human trait.
It’s a smart, entertaining variation on a familiar formula. It’s clever without being smug, scary without losing its sense of humor, and messy in the most enjoyable way.
a confident, intelligent crime thriller driven by strong performances and a director who clearly trusts his audience. It’s stylish without being showy, thoughtful without becoming inaccessible.
For viewers willing to embrace a stylised, modernised interpretation rather than a traditional period drama, this Wuthering Heights offers a lurid, provocative and strangely compelling ride.
The Straight Story may be understated to a fault, but it resists everything that is cloying, cliched and trite with superlative naturalism.

With an impressive cast and solid premise, this is perfectly suited for a quick, late-night horror fix. However, if you are looking for a film to stimulate the brain or inject some new life into the genre, you may want to look elsewhere.
Everyone should seek out Cookie Queens. It will put a smile on your face and remind you there is still plenty to feel good about when it comes to the future.

An incredible film, one that will stay with you for a long time. It is a difficult watch and deals with deeply troubling subject matter, but it is handled with such care and precision that it is hard to imagine it being done any better.
As debuts go, it’s a confident and distinctive one, marking Bryn Chainey as a filmmaker with a strong feel for atmosphere and an ear for the unsettling sounds hidden in everyday life.

A sensory delight and a prime example of deft storytelling meeting a perfect ensemble. A genre-defying fairytale that perfectly melds themes of love and loss with those of betrayal and beginnings. It’s one of the best films of the year.
If you’re a Statham devotee looking for your next action fix, Shelter delivers exactly what you’re signed up for. Just don’t go in expecting it to reinvent the wheel

This is stylish, entertaining chaos and undeniably fun, it never quite lets the audience fully suspend disbelief. The idea is clever and original, but the film keeps reminding you just how much everyone is expected to buy into the absurdity.
Bold, strange, romantic, and deeply human, the film is elevated by a wonderful script, gorgeous costumes, and an ensemble cast that fully commits to the heightened reality of the story.

A gripping, often brutal exploration of power, control, and inequality. Even when its thematic ambitions falter, its pacing, performances and relentless tension ensure it remains a deeply unsettling offering from Raimi.
Only Two Can Play might be a footnote in Sellers’ career, but it is an interesting display of his talents and a minor snapshot of kitchen sink Britain.
Fun, unhinged - Buddy accomplishes exactly what it sets out to do. It is hilarious, unique, and wildly unpredictable, becoming a true Sundance original.
Ultimately, Mercy isn’t aggressively bad, it's just really dumb. It borrows the aesthetic of superior sci-fi films, without grasping the soul of the genre.
Quite enjoyable to watch, but nothing more.

This is a harrowing, thoughtful, and impeccably crafted film that enriches its franchise while standing powerfully on its own. It is a real triumph for DaCosta in one of her biggest and best films yet.
Flawlessly acted, beautifully shot, heart-achingly moving and affecting, at times rip-roaringly exciting and incomparably and unashamedly nostalgic.
Silly, campy and beyond bonkers.

For long-time fans, it represents a compelling new chapter; for newcomers, it remains a visually arresting invitation, albeit one that benefits from familiarity with the franchise’s long and layered history.
This is a confident, quietly unnerving debut, bolstered by restrained performances and a purposeful lo-fi aesthetic.
Its charm lies less in its high concept than in the simple, very human story about what it means to love and be loved.
Marty Supreme is intense, daring and full of confidence, with Chalamet delivering his best performance to date.
Jankel’s direction is assured, the period detail immersive, and the performances committed, but where Desperate Journey falters is in its reliance on well-worn wartime tropes.

Despite its compromises, it has a heart that’s grown 3 sizes bigger than certain critics would have you believe. And therefore, though it has never put a scrap of gold in my pocket, I say it has done me good, and will do me good and I say God bless it.
With Hawke’s exceptional performance at its center, the film earns its place as a poignant, quietly powerful character study.
Powered by Akshay Kumar’s reliable comic timing and a world that’s as chaotic as it is colourful, this one doesn’t quite become a classic, but it keeps the fun going while it lasts.

There are moments of wit and absurdity that remind you of what the film could have been, but they arrive a little too sporadically. In the end, it's a one-time watch that works in bursts, without fully coming together as a sharply toasted whole.
Dacoit’s biggest flaw is how relentlessly generic its storytelling feels.
There are flaws, but the charm of the protagonist and the visual magic are enough to compensate for that in what is arguably the best big-screen experience this year so far.
It may not be as memorable and cool as Dhurandhar 1, but it does enough to justify why this story was stretched into a two-part saga.
Overall, Jab Khuli Kitaab means well and often signals its intentions loudly. What it lacks is the emotional depth to make those intentions truly land.

For a while, it teases the possibility of becoming a gripping drama anchored by a magnetic Anil. But as the narrative continues, the film seems unsure of what it wants to say or where it wants to land.
Uneven chemistry and a finale that lacks the sting it promises dilute the impact of what could have been a far more provocative film.
Whether one agrees with its politics or not, what is undeniable is that nuance is sacrificed at the altar of impact. And when outrage becomes the aim, the medium suffers as much as the message.

It is no miracle that only a woman could tell this story, not once but twice. If the novel gave Agnes the space to breathe, Chloé Zhao takes a step further, holding her hand as she navigates an entire spectrum of life's many unfair revelations.
Margot Robbie and Jacob Elordi are miscast in this highly sexualised and stupidly melodramatic reimagination by Emerald Fennell.

The film does not have enough meat to pack a feature-length without becoming repetitive and packed with tropes. You can see each plot twist and character death from a mile away, and it’s not like the film tries to hide them.

This is a film that haunts the audience, just like it haunts the protagonist. A slow burn that keeps you engaged, Kennedy is as much about the anticipation as it is about the bang, to paraphrase the great Alfred Hitchcock.
Assi has all the right ingredients to be a powerful film, and in flashes, it truly is. The problem lies not in what the film wants to say, but in how consistently it manages to say it, with clarity.
It is watchable, even fun in parts, but rarely affecting in the way Bhardwaj’s best work is. You walk out entertained in flashes... and strangely unmoved.

Bejoy blends social contrast and creature-feature thrills into an occasionally messy, but largely gripping ride. Even when it borders on the absurd, the film stays effective enough to keep you invested.

media_title: Bhabiji Ghar Par Hain: Fun on the Run
rt_quote: While the characters remain endearing in parts, the screenplay offers nothing new to justify the jump from television to cinema. It ends up being less a film and more a reminder that some humour is best enjoyed in short, controlled doses.
For viewers who enjoy slow-burn crime thrillers driven by character rather than spectacle, this sequel offers enough to stay engaged.
As the film unfolds in its chaotic, unbridled energy, it becomes a portrait of governmental failure, rampant corruption, and the price one pays to run away.
Filmmakers Biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazić are issuing a compassionate call for preservation here, a necessary reminder of how co-dependent human livelihoods are.
Shame and Money is a plea for the many Shabans and Hatixhes who endure and carry on, hoping the next day will be a little easier.
Iconic filmmaker Barbara Hammer is very much alive and unforgettable in this new documentary that is largely built on archival material.
De Araújo has made a blistering, gripping film that demands unblinking attention. Josephine is a stone-cold triumph, and one of the year's first great films.
Unflinchingly honest from the very first frame, One in a Million is a masterful document of a family trying to find a place to call home.
Nuisance Bear is a radical piece of non-fiction filmmaking, subverting the viewer's gaze to interrogate the difference between protection and exploitation, morality and activism.

This chapter works less as a shock and more as a statement of continuity. Mardaani 3 may not be the sharpest entry in the series, but it is a sobering reminder that Shivani’s fight, much like the crimes it confronts, is far from over.

The film rests on Palmer's face, who breathtakingly charts Sid's journey from heartbreak to anxiety and everything in between. She is the life force that propels this coming-of-age drama into unforgettable territory.
Even when the film shakes, Jennifer Lawrence holds it tight. She delivers a soul-baring, utterly breathtaking performance.
A film like this needed more sensitivity and nuance, but what we get feels performative.
While its excesses are hard to ignore, so is its sincerity. The film reaches back into a time when patriotism in cinema was worn unapologetically... when heroes spoke loudly and emotions rang true.
Ultimately, a handful of performances and cameos manage to inject fleeting energy, but they cannot compensate for humour that feels thinly stretched in Happy Patel.
Varun and Pulkit as Rahu-Ketu try their best, but most of what they do feels improv rather than intentionally comic. Almost as if they were trying hard to make the unfunny bits work.
Anchored by deeply humane turns from Hugh and Kate, it may be old-fashioned in spirit, but it carries enough emotional truth to earn its place well beyond nostalgia.
The Raja Saab’s aim might be to make you laugh, but the overall film needed more profundity and brilliance.
Its heart is in the right place, and Benedict’s performance alone makes it worth engaging with, yet the film’s insistence on externalising pain in such an overbearing way keeps viewers at a distance.

Overall, Ikkis works best when it stops trying to be a war film and becomes a painful reminder. It tells you something unbearable: that our freedoms were bought by people who never got to live theirs.

Anaconda understands that not every film needs to say something profound — but it forgets that it still needs to be entertaining. Its self-awareness mistakes recognition for critique, and nostalgia for purpose.

media_title: Tu Meri Main Tera Main Tera Tu Meri
rt_quote: You might stay for the warmth of the veterans, but you will leave still searching for the love the title promised.

There is nothing inherently wrong with a tearjerker, and Goodbye June earns many of its emotional beats through craft and calibre alone. Yet its carefully arranged grief, polished warmth and preordained reconciliations keep it at arm’s length.
No Other Choice is a film of acute sensibility and ambition, and further cements the status of Park Chan-wook as one of our greatest living filmmakers.

media_title: The Sun Rises on Us All
rt_quote: Zhilei delivers a rich and nuanced performance, marked by unvarnished emotional complexity.
Jim Jarmusch's latest film is charming and might initially seem too simple for its own good, but it has a lovely wisdom that lingers.
Djukić has made a richly atmospheric and sensual film, one that never fetishises the untangling of Lucia's sexuality. It gives her space and lets her breathe.
None of these girls comes under any judgment, and the film offers them space and a warmth of community that carries them through.
The film's metamorphosis in the third act is rather heavy-handed, and unfortunately, incurious in the manner it deals with substance abuse.
The Sound of Falling pushes and challenges the limits of visual inquiry, as the film also transforms as if we are being watched.
It is a film that is not just about one country, but arrives like a warning to authoritarian regimes everywhere, a signal for citizens of the world.

media_title: If I Had Legs I'd Kick You
rt_quote: Rose Byrne's volcanic performance anchors the film.
The Mastermind is a political film in the realist, most gripping manner, which intends to knock its protagonist- and in extension, the viewer- sideways.
Paula Beer shines in this psychological drama infused with mystery and wisdom, that rewards the viewer as it unfolds.
Legend's flaws are sometimes overwhelming, yet on the whole, the frosting is so splendid it's easy to overlook the lack of cake.
Simply put, this movie couldn't suck worse if it tried.

It's a measure of Cruise's magnificent agitation that Zellweger -- bursting with nervous tics and grimaces that leave you unsure whether she's a terrific or terrible actress but equally forbid you to forget her -- comes off as the calm one.
Thin on plot and lavishly nuanced.
Other than their performances and the eye-pleasing 1930s art deco sets, there is nothing instructive enough, much less lively enough, to recommend.
On a purely technical level, especially with Frank Stanley's excellent cinematography, this picture easily outjumps and outshoots Grease 1. But so what?
You can't identify with the victims -- they're too stupid; and you can't identify with the monsters -- they're too artificial.
The sequel is troubled by an internal struggle between the impulse to make the story mean something and the impulse to make it mean as little as possible.
Waiting for Guffman is never mean-spirited. Its weird warmth is perfectly embodied by Guest himself.
RoboCop has the strutting pleasures of good genre filmmaking.

Thompson plucks out the novelist's delicate wit, while Lee, a master of domestic dramady, takes Austen gently over the top in a prankish farce with just enough heartburn to elicit the occasional covert sob.

It's a gorgeously detailed mood piece about an unlikely meeting of souls that results in a life transformed by, of all things, metaphor. Comparisons with the crowdpleaser Cinema Paradiso will inevitably abound, but Il Postino's sweetness flows less coyly.
This is the best mainstream film yet about kids for kids.

A pleasure from start to finish, Muppet Treasure Island orchestrates people, puppets, shameless gags and sublimely ridiculous production numbers to wryly rework Robert Louis Stevenson's classic kids' tale.

It’s like watching dance, and it’s beautiful, and when, in the last half-hour, the movie drops the smug, pseudo-hip jokiness that mars the script and settles into pure romantic tragedy, you’re along, body and soul, for the ride.
At once the most beautiful and most disappointing movie of the year. For it could have been great, and had it been great it might have changed a few of us here below.
Perhaps, along the way, Rob Reiner's inner child got trampled, smothered under all that borscht-belt waggery.
Reiner and screenwriter Aaron Sorkin may be reaching for '30s-style banterama, but what they end up with is a '50s-style romantic simper with two hopelessly miscast leads.
Misery zips right along, propelled by its queasy, cruel humor, and by its two fine stars.
Rob Reiner's direction is subtle and precise as it was on Spinal Tap, and he gives us a host of standout supporting characters and performances that deserve films of their own.

We've yawned through the demographically perfect bliss of studio films for so long that The Princess Bride... seems too good to be true. But director Rob Reiner and writer William Goldman awaken us from our slumber with a jolt of pure Hollywood magic.

Neither Spielberg nor his writers can be accused of exploiting the idea without caring about it: they do care about it, up to a point. But that's the point at which they simply don't know what to do with it.
This is the movie of somebody interested in having a tongue-in-cheek good time with an American obsession, no more and no less. It's a fast ride in a hot car.
Technically agile and graced with some perfectly good acting, Big Top Pee-wee doesn't exactly succeed as a comedy, because its theme is so weird and incongruous.
A solid-looking structure from a distance, when you get close enough to see it, you discover that the movie's not only chocolate but hollow.
It's more of a waltz through espionage lite, with a real tango thrown in to cement its stamp of sophistication.
As an adventure story, The Abyss is pretty good.
In the end, what's scariest about this movie isn't the T-1000 or the evocation of nuclear holocaust - it's that even Cameron's most violent excesses are a helluva lot of fun to watch.

You'll be able to guess the twist if you've ever read a Marvel Comic, but the plot isn't the attraction here, it's the action. Arnold takes a licking and keeps on ticking in a performance that's chilly con carnage.
Schwarzenegger's consolidated all of his most audience-pleasing traits into one perfectly packaged product -- 90 percent brawn and 10 percent wiseacre.

As good and committed as Jennifer Lawrence is, there were times I wanted to rescue her from her own movie, to protect her from the fate of Faye Dunaway when “Mommie Dearest” turned another blond Oscar winner into a joke.

Instead of just splicing together Rambo and Aliens, these dudes have spent untold millions producing a fight between Arnold Schwarzenegger and a special effect that succeeds on a slam-bang visceral level but doesn't even attempt anything else.
You will look in vain for Arnold Schwarzenegger... You will look in vain for many things.
From Beyond is exemplary.
It's precisely as art that Desert Hearts fails most dismally.
This movie is about what movies should be about. It's about politics and screwing, fighting and making money, guilt and love and anger; it's about the juice and blood that make life worthwhile.
Too bad the resulting film is not a landmark, or, for that matter, particularly new.
Excellent. The best movie I have ever seen about being young in the world tat rock 'n' roll sings to.
What holds the hold thing together -- gives it the dreamy distant look of a fairy tale, and the familiarity of a folk tale -- is Hill's beautifully visual direction.
Boogie Nights is a big, bold movie not just because it embraces nearly a decade's worth of human drama, but because it is a wildly, belligerently cinematic creation.
Although at times the film is inches away from being undermined by its own sweetness, it sleeps with the quietest of anger, showing us that it isn't necessary to shriek in order to subvert.
Paul Thomas Anderson's stylish, noirish feature debut so transcends its worn-out plot that for a while you believe you're seeing a film about something important: goodness, no less.
The remake can't possibly avoid appearing thin and a bit silly.
Tom Hanks, Tim Allen and Don Rickles lend voices that are ably directed by John Lasseter.
The best film about rock and roll ever.
The actors can't make us feel for Peyton, because they aren't given the tools to do it with. And if we don't care about Peyton, Darkman hardly makes sense.
Mortal Kombat isn't the worst movie of the year, but it's easily the most forgettable.

Sentimental Value circles back to themes Trier and Vogt have explored throughout their careers: siblings and parentification, houses as sites of memory and trauma, and the complicated roles that parents play in their children’s lives.

media_title: I'm Not Everything I Want to Be
rt_quote: Tasovská’s film is formally ambitious and accomplished — creative nonfiction at its best. She crafts a dynamic narrative through clever sound and pacing despite being built solely on still photographs.

"Keeping her camera at the height of the young students and close to them, Simon immediately helps us forge an empathic connection with the young people. The adults, by contrast, are giants whose top half often doesn’t fit into the frame."

"The new 4K restoration of Charles Burnett’s delightful 1999 late-in-life screwball comedy offers this worthy film a new lease on life, much like its characters...The film’s zany premise gives way to a touching story of two lonely people."

Pauline Loquès’s heartrending feature debut, Nino, beautifully and viscerally captures that strange limbo you enter when you get a serious medical diagnosis, like treatable cancer...Loquès finds a thoughtful cinematic language for Nino’s alienation

The world of The Girl with the Needle is a sinister one, where husbands can disappear in the war without a trace, and you can be thrown out of your home or your job with a moment’s notice...one of the year’s hardest watches and also one of its very best.
Fillières’ hugely witty and very funny film tells Barberie’s story of trying to find a new lease on life with tenderness and aplomb.

An impressive debut film from Indonesian filmmaker Tumpal Tampubolon, Crocodile Tears is a horror-inflected story of a too-close relationship between a mother and her adult son...who is trying to break free from her clutches.

Collaboratively made with multiple directors, the powerful, urgent, and incisive No Other Land serves as an excellent introduction to the Israeli settler-colonial state in Palestine...The panoply of perspectives...is its greatest strength and weakness.

[Shoeshine] is still resonant, humanist, and infuriating today. It’s the story of a friendship torn apart by the cruel and indifferent adult world that cares little for children and less for the challenges of post-war poverty.
Ann Hui’s July Rhapsody is a melodrama about marital discord with a light touch, where both partners explore other relationships.
This warm and tender film that manages to be a feel-good movie, which only occasionally dips into sentimentality amidst the tragic subject matter.

The film is about coping with what happens when boundaries have been so irreparably breached you don’t even know what is appropriate anymore. Tennis, with its carefully outlined court and rules about what is in and out of bounds, is an excellent metaphor.

Japanese-French filmmaker Koya Kamura’s impressive feature debut, Winter in Sokcho, is a story about a place, a young woman’s search for identity and place in the world, and a brief encounter between a visiting French artist and a Korean hotel worker.

Egil Pederson’s My Father’s Daughter begins with a sort of Looking for Eric premise before expanding into a very thoughtful, often funny, coming-of-ager about the search for identity and the impossibility of ever really finding it.
This sensitively made feature from Senez is a character study about a father who isn’t allowed to be a father, an unjust system that won’t allow joint custody, and the people caught within it.

Slow is a tender, crushing film about two people in love who struggle to make their relationship work. Elena and Dovydas are instantly smitten with each other but run into a roadblock when Dovydas clarifies that he’s asexual.
Like Flee, the animation in Pelikan Blue anonymizes the forgers and their customers while also bringing us into the memories rather than merely listening to the documentary-recorded voices.
Veronika Franz and Severin Fiala’s harrowing new drama makes their previous chillers, Goodnight Mommy and The Lodge, look like episodes of Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood.

You’d be justified in thinking that leads Kristen Stewart and Katy O’Brian are headed for a bad romance. They are. They’re also impeccable players in a wry, drug-fueled thriller where the obsessive rush of first love is the real narcotic.

"If The Old Oak is, as Loach has been threatening, really Loach’s final film, it will be a strong summation of his work: a film about community and solidarity in places you wouldn’t expect from people who can barely care for themselves."

media_title: I Don't Know Who You Are
rt_quote: "I Don’t Know Who You Are, the first feature film from M. H. Murray, does for access to PEP what Never Rarely Sometimes Always did for abortion access."

"By presenting us with heroes we can’t care about and a de facto villain who is the only character with a pulse in the film, Cronenberg keeps a film about a politically charged topic apolitical and hard to invest in."

The plot of All Your Faces is schematic and mostly predictable, and you can feel the gears clicking into place. But Henry compensates for this with well-written, complex characters and excellent performances.

Stéphane Brizé’s latest entry in his cinema of sad, desperate men (The Measure of a Man, At War), Out of Season, is a lovely little film about a depressed actor, Mathieu. who temporarily rekindles an old flame while decompressing at a spa in Quiberon.

For all Yau’s good intentions as the project’s director, screenwriter, producer and sole investor, his formally unruly piece of social critique is often undermined by its melodramatic portrayal of the banality of evil.

Viewers with the patience to sit through a deliberately paced hour of shady encounters in dingy nightclubs and snow-driven back alleys will be richly rewarded by a second half showcasing some of the best heroic bloodshed in recent memory.
They Will Kill You is a delicious slice of pure midnight movie madness.

media_title: Ready or Not 2: Here I Come
rt_quote: Ready or Not 2: Here I Come is a follow-up devoid of original ideas and too reliant on bone-crunching violence.

Ciao UFO proves a remarkably effective piece of storytelling, resonating both as a touching character drama and as an elegy for a vanished "golden age" that now exists only in [Hong Kong’s] collective memory.

The film boasts an ambitious array of vibrant DIY visual effects. These impressive renderings of the in-game world make this otherwise conventional, dream-chasing story far more infectious than it has any right to be.
Ryan Gosling flies almost entirely solo in Project Hail Mary, a disappointingly derivative sci-fi mash-up of Interstellar, The Martian and Tom Hanks’ desert island drama Cast Away.
Though it hardly marks a creative breakthrough for the director, Girlfriends lingers as an intimate portrait of a woman looking back to find her way forward.

Viewers who like their cops-and-robbers thrillers loud, frenetic and illogical are in for a blast with Ultimate Revenge, an unabashedly derivative addition to Hong Kong’s once-feted action cinema tradition.
Hoppers manages a perfect high-wire act, working both as a thoroughly entertaining family film and something rich with adult themes.
While this nifty premise sets up a series of absorbing set pieces, the screenplay proves convoluted and confusing, frequently mistaking a lack of information for mystery and intrigue.
One cannot help but feel it is all a bit of a hodgepodge, as the filmmaker throws everything at the anime wall to see what sticks.
Panda Plan: The Magical Tribe defies all expectations as a marked improvement on its predecessor in almost every conceivable way.
It is a beautiful conclusion to this loose 13-year trilogy, proving Chen has fully matured as a filmmaker.
Blades of the Guardians may not rank among the greatest wuxia films ever made, but it is easily one of the fiercest entries we have had in years.
Despite the disjointed pacing and glitzy packaging, Night King remains fun to watch and offers a largely crowd-pleasing spectacle of survival against the odds.

media_title: The Snowball on a Sunny Day
rt_quote: Part sweet tear-jerker, part love letter to Hong Kong cinema and the craft of filmmaking, this Lunar New Year offering reveals an unexpectedly whimsical side of the writer-director Philip Yung.

Fennell’s take on Emily Bronte’s 1847 novel Wuthering Heights has the substance to back it up. Beautifully costumed, designed, shot and performed, the film is an impeccably made tale of doomed lovers, one that will bring a tear to the eye.

Even at 84, Baisho remains a magnetic screen presence, drawing us in with a performance that deftly sidesteps histrionic grandstanding in favour of a subtle humanity to make Tokyo Taxi an utterly captivating ride.
Akimoto proves here that he has a unique and exciting visual sensibility, capable of elevating an otherwise conventional exercise in sci-fi escapism into a work rich with bold artistic flourish.
Fans of Raimi’s trademark comic gore will get a kick out of the excess.
The film is tense and, at its best, depicts an eerily familiar world, where drones, body cams, mobile phones and doorbell cameras capture our every move.

Short on action but long on ham-fisted life lessons, the debut feature from writer-director Li Taiyan seems tailor-made for the Chinese holiday season, with its fast-paced blend of slapstick humour, domestic squabbles and climactic melodrama.
By championing the heroism and sacrifices of ordinary civilians, and shifting focus away from patriotic rhetoric to intimate character dynamics, the film proves surprisingly entertaining.

Fans of stripped-down, unmuzzled Friday-night bloodletting will have a grand old time, as Ben’s frenzied antics result in a procession of face-rippings, skull-crushings and other unflinchingly feral deaths.
It is a testament to the cast’s skill that they manage to wring moments of genuine emotion from such heavy-handed material, which mistakes grimness for profundity.
DaCosta’s morally complex thriller sets us up for a grandstand finish.
The terrible burden of grief is laid bare in The Thing with Feathers, a gloomy but undeniably touching drama.
A subpar historical sci-fi fantasy that is saved – and arguably even transcended – by the potent wave of nostalgia it inspires in its target audience.
This feel-good, family-friendly offering defies expectations with its infectious positivity and cheeky humour.
A beautifully staged and delicately poised rumination on the parallels between writing and travel.

Under Current is a quintessential example of the Hong Kong crime film in its present, transitional state. While it paints a mostly watchable portrait of greed and corruption, the film’s story also happens to be thoroughly detached from reality.

Road to Vendetta, a violent, John Wick-inspired action thriller co-produced by Hong Kong and Japan, delivers as a pop idol vehicle with its ample visual style. [But] the film’s screenplay appears multiple revisions away from telling a convincing story.

Acting accolades may naturally follow Liew in the coming awards season, although it will be fascinating to see where Tam’s directing career goes next after such a daring, sensitive work that stays so true to her own vision.
It is not "Pixar at its peak" levels, but Zootopia 2 will delight kids craving a bit of pre-Christmas sparkle.
This hot-blooded but generic tale about perseverance works better as a record of Cheung’s sheer determination to reinvent himself than as the artistic breakout that he had hoped it would be.

While Against All Odds is smaller and scrappier than most recent Chinese war movies, Lau’s bold endeavour punches well above its weight and makes the compelling case that an engaging story is always worth fighting for.

Anchored by an astonishing central performance from Ryo Yoshizawa and a fastidious devotion to the traditional art of kabuki theatre, Lee Sang-il’s sumptuous saga Kokuho emerges as the finest Japanese film of the year.

media_title: Now You See Me: Now You Don't
rt_quote: Despite the convincing sleight of hand, conjuring excitement is one thing this film fails to do.

Hung’s ambitious screenplay poses some legitimate moral quandaries about the value of one life against another. ... Unfortunately, 96 Minutes lacks the narrative dexterity to draw much of a conclusion beyond revenge definitely being bad.

While the innocent looks of its two protagonists and the Japanese anime-inspired fantasy action scenes might suggest otherwise, Another World is a morally complex film that repeatedly challenges its characters with circumstances of extreme evil.
With Hawke’s bogeyman right up there with some of cinema’s most terrifying villains, this is an unsettling addition to Derrickson’s impressive canon.

This high-concept fantasy romance ... asks its audience to succumb to the supposedly poetic swooning of its star-crossed lovers – only to make it a very tall order indeed with a criminally underdeveloped set-up and an unfathomably illogical plot.

To focus on the convoluted, nearly kaleidoscopic story... would be to miss the pleasures of this ambitious effort, which oozes dark humour in its often cynical dialogue and boasts spectacular production design that renders every location a little surreal.

Packed with jumps, scares, skin-crawling stand-offs and breathless belly laughs, Dollhouse emerges as a delightful surprise, while Nagasawa leads a cast of accomplished veterans in a committed performance of unwavering confusion and abject terror.
A riotously entertaining black comedy about the nature of truth, the power of propaganda and the delicate intricacies of international cooperation.

While the decision to shoot the gameplay scenes in live action is a refreshing way to convey the virtual experience, Good Game is otherwise too conceptually lightweight and artificially inspirational in its telling of the players’ personal stories.

Compared to this, Anderson’s last two outings – the Pynchon-derived Inherent Vice and Licorice Pizza – were lightweight efforts. One Battle After Another finds the director at the peak of his power and is sure to be an awards contender.
Yeon sets up a fascinating premise. ... Where the film falls down spectacularly, however, is by failing to reconcile these intriguing threads into a satisfying conclusion.

This feature debut by Kwan Man-hin is confident enough to rely on the strength of its likeable leads and not succumb to cheap humour. The Remnant is a largely engaging watch, its uneven pacing offset by a narrative that takes fairly surprising turns.
One of the most provocative, entertaining TV movies ever.
RoboCop 3 is a senseless, dreary and rambling mess of a fantasy-action film.
...side-splitting tribute to earnest showmanship and all-American bad taste.

How can romantic love make itself known in a world where the heart must submit to the yoke of manners and custom? Yes, this is Jane Austen territory, and in Sense and Sensibility, it's a handsome, engaging and surprisingly warm place to visit.

Troisi, Noiret and company relate this heartwarming and lustrous story to perfection, even though, sadly, the offscreen finale surpasses in sentiment what this delightful motion picture so sensitively offers.
It's bloody, witless and mind-numbing.
Gracefully blending raucous comedy with intense drama, the film is about the loss of innocence as well as the getting of wisdom.
Schwarzenegger, Curtis, Arnold and Paxton are perfect, as is the supporting cast of heavies and henchpeople.
While one can admire the daunting risk it took to get the movie made, The Abyss proves too big and unwieldy an epic.

If this Terminator is an indestructible cyborg who can eviscerate human weaklings with his bare hands, what does he need guns for? James Cameron, writer-director of The Terminator, is an efficiency expert. More deaths per minute.
Here's an uninteresting variation on a dumb idea: a remake of a bad movie.
Strong production values, impressive special effects and a super-human performance by Danny Glover make Predator 2 an occasionally effective, but awkwardly conceived sci-fi sequel.
Don't look for good acting, believable dialogue, character development or, heaven forbid, a plot. But gobs of gore and special effects, yes.
The best film yet made about love between two women. It's good-humored, well constructed, and refreshingly free of the morose contemplation and doubt that usually accompanies treatment of this theme.
A visual amazing fantasy.
Night of the Living Dead is a redundancy upon itself.
More than a tale of a young boy's playthings that come to life and interact when no one is around, Toy Story ingeniously taps into the stream of childhood recollections and emotions.
Mortal Kombat is like being inside, well, a video game. Which is exactly the point, I suppose, but it's still not much of a movie.

media_title: The Return of the Living Dead
rt_quote: Abysmal tongue-in cheek horror film.
[A] tale of zany invention and fascinating images.
The lessons for children are numerous; the most refreshing is that not every movie must revolve around toy-store tie-ins.

media_title: DuckTales, the Movie: Treasure of the Lost Lamp
rt_quote: Thankfully short on violence, and most other risque ingredients that populate so many films.
Derivative ideas, an uneven central performance and awkward handling of the elements by director Joe Dante hurt this film.
Heaven knows what the filmmakers spent on Supergirl, but regardless of the amount it wasn't enough to give wing to this mediocre adventure.
Romero had all the ingredients of making a colorful spoof on the first two pictures, but rigor mortis quickly set in.
Director/co-screenwriter Walter Murch tells his story at the right pace, never getting so bogged down in one dilemma as to forget a crisis in the making somewhere else.
The screenplay may be a mess, but De Palma's expert direction, combined with Cruise's starpower and Industrial Light and Magic's special-effects sorcery, makes this a Mission worth accepting.

media_title: Star Wars: Episode VI - Return of the Jedi
rt_quote: Dramatically, Return of the Jedi disappoints. In a sense, the narrative has boxed itself into a corner -- characters introduced and developed in the first two films are unwaveringly established in this one, so that there is no room for them to grow.

media_title: Star Wars: Episode I - The Phantom Menace
rt_quote: The film introduces too many characters and develops them too little.
The Wedding Banquet is a wonderful dramatic comedy.
Aladdin has just enough of all the right elements, including a winning series of songs by the late Howard Ashman, Alan Menken and Tim Rice. It's a family film in the truest sense of the term.
Beetlejuice entertains, in a very peculiar way. Nothing quite like it has come along before.
It should satisfy devotees and compel a new batch of aficionados to scurry off for videos of the previous movies. And is the hatch door left ajar for a fifth installment of the saga? Definitely.
Imagine my dismay to find Alien 3 not merely less accomplished than its predecessors, but a complete violation of the spirit of the earlier movies.
Gillian Armstrong's exceedingly lovely version is a glorious achievement in every respect.

Tim Robbins delivers a distinguished performance, with Morgan Freeman equally marvelous. This is that rare movie occurrence that has the ability to sweep the viewer into an alien universe; it is superior filmmaking on any level.
Dull, talky and jam-packed with terrible performances, who knows which witch is which in the whammyless Teen Witch.
The result is that rare thing, a movie that is in every way an improvement upon the book.
A razor-sharp, brutal look at violence, racism and alienation.
Hang on tight for a real mind-blower, with astonishing visual effects, frightening monsters and exciting stunt fights, as the film inexorably reveals the terrifying answer to "What is the Matrix?"
The Color Purple is that rarity in American films -- a faithful adaptation of a stirring book. To watch it is to laugh and cry with characters that you'll not soon forget.
Viewers who want the bitter taste of Kane's Batman character in a world of gloom and doom may like this animated film, but it is hardly family entertainment.

media_title: Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom
rt_quote: This film reconfirms Spielberg's status as a master movie story teller. My only frustration in seeing this film is that I wish I were 10 years old again, though [Spielberg's] gift is to coax the child out of the moviegoer.
Because of an irreverent and wholly enthusiastic performance, Campbell makes the film far more than it should be.
It's an able comedy despite the heavy topics touched on throughout.
Alma's Rainbow is ambitious and occasionally fun. Unfortunately, director Chenzira's meandering script becomes diluted and confusing when it should have simplified an essentially interesting story.
This sweetly surrealist comedy is, arguably, Murray's most irresistible effort. Groundhog Day is a warm and rewarding story about reason, reckoning, and romance.
TNT is to be applauded for adapting a great summer read into a fine summer watch.

Brooks proves himself to be an actor's director. He understands the nuances of behavior between characters. It is these small moments that make Terms of Endearment worth seeing, in spite of its meanderings.

It is hard to imagine a more serious or heartfelt exploration of the inner conflicts faced by Jesus. Charges of blasphemy leveled against the film by some Christian leaders are hard to square with the filmmakers' obvious reverence.
[Mabel] insists on showing us the birds and the trees, but the sincerity ultimately shows up in a remarkable manner
We enter the film hopping to particular conclusions, and we leave just looking for somebunny to hug.
The film’s narrative prowess comes from its unique integration of documentary and fictional storytelling, creating a cinematic vernacular that is both poignant and refreshing.

By portraying racism as more of an annoyance than a tragedy, the movie gives its characters (and audience) permission to let loose and have fun, away from a patriarchal surveillance state that masquerades as "community" and "culture."
If there’s one film recently that has reminded me of why we go to the movies — indeed, why I persist in writing about film — it’s Chloé Zhao’s Hamnet.
[The] dense narrative complexity creates the right platform for much of the abstractions that arise within the film, giving the philosophical meanderings something to cling to.
Part disaster movie, part dystopian technothriller, and part teenage coming-of-age story, Neo Sora’s Happyend blends these seemingly disparate genres to form an affecting tale of friendship and love.
Rabbit Trap doesn’t exactly snap to break bones, but it does its best to make a long-lasting impression.
Zane captures that restlessness with uncanny precision.

media_title: Little Amélie or the Character of Rain
rt_quote: With a tender hand, Little Amélie tackles darker topics as well, unafraid to delve into death, loss, trauma, and even distrust.
For viewers who respond to character-first cinema about the costs of making a life in a city that constantly recalibrates who belongs, [Lucky Lu] is worth your time.
[Riz Ahmed] provides a compelling performance as the anguished young prince, but the director relies too heavily on his star and forgets to build up a believably corrupt and complex world around him.
A hypnotic, uncompromising vision with a shorter runtime and more approachable than Diaz’s eight-hour epics, yet no less resonant.
Hayakawa’s coming-of-age leaves behind something subtler: the impression of a summer where life and death pressed against each other, and a girl who tried to make space for both.
At its best, 'Vice Is Broke' shows the contradiction at Vice’s core. For all its swagger about counterculture, Vice was built on something almost embarrassingly ordinary: the desire to belong.
Nisha Ganatra doesn’t reinvent the freaky wheel, but Freakier Friday gives fans of the original movie the nostalgia Gen X and millennials crave, while being enough Gen Z to bring in a new audience.

Stranger Eyes grips audiences in that low-grade dread kind of way, the kind of menace you don’t feel until it settles into your chest. But then Yeo does something strange, almost counterintuitive: he downshifts.
Amidst magnetic performances, laughter riots, and fun action sequences, 'Aavesham' changes colours many times, unveiling a touching exploration of male vulnerability.
Iintimate and artful in equal measure.
Meditatively paced with achingly beautiful visuals
The film brilliantly illustrates anger and horror’s ability to compound exponentially within relationships.
The patience of this film is its masterwork.
An intimate and poetic ode to youth.
A quiet indictment of the ways that the systems have failed vulnerable refugees and their families.
Endlessly watchable for the giddy joy it takes in parody
The film is anchored by the quiet yet powerful performance by Choi as the model-minority-myth-busting So-young.
The themes presented in 'Noise' are far greater in theory than in execution.
By following the Siev family through the troubled lockdowns, 'Bad Axe' utilizes the power of observation in watching them work tirelessly for their community.
Bang and Scarpellino are instantly charming.
A brilliant example of the thriller genre.
A shocking revelation of stolen childhoods, unhappy family dynamics, and combative sexual politics.
Mighty, weighty, important, and unmissable.
Come for the food porn; stay for the outrageous rom-com twists
A compelling and revealing look into real-life online drama and the ongoing struggle of trans people in the Philippines.
A fabulistic examination of women pushed to bizarre and harmful behaviours by the restrictive society around them.
The film excels most at its eruptions of the frayed family bonds, where it moves into its most deeply specific moments.
There’s an attempt from Liu to come off as charming, but, not unlike his Twitter feed, it just ends up feeling cringe-worthy.

media_title: What's Love Got to Do with It?
rt_quote: Although there is definite chemistry between James and Latif, the dynamics set up between their characters do not serve the themes of the movie quite so well.
[The film] understands that healing is a long-term process and thus doesn’t offer clear-cut resolutions, but rather the potential of such.
This film is not afraid to pull its punches.
So dynamic is [Lkhagvadulam Purev-Ochir's] visual storytelling that it can help one overlook some of the rougher patches.
At once enjoyable and inspiring in the way its protagonist finds a new lease on life in the most unexpected of ways.
It’s a film that could easily have got bogged down in sadness, but Rebuilding is more interested in the resilience of its land and its people, and in lighting a path through tough times.
The ideal fit for our social media obsessed age, a time of extreme content and quests for perfection. The Drama shows us the horror behind a carefully cultivated façade.
La Grazia is a completely compelling and stimulating piece of cinema, one that puts being sensible on a pedestal and that feels like fantasy more than it should.
Goddard’s script is phenomenally funny and to say no one could have pulled this off better than Gosling is a huge understatement.
The Bride! is a sometimes seductive, sometimes frustrating watch, a star-stuffed feast that leaves you hungry.
With political instability spreading across the globe, this hangdog hero speaks powerfully to us all.

Screenwriters Hunter Andrews and Eoin Doran paint a depressingly credible picture of an overstretched and inhumane institution that makes it as difficult as possible for people to turn their lives around.

media_title: If I Had Legs I'd Kick You
rt_quote: Byrne takes what could have been a highly dislikeable, unforgivably reckless character and renders her compelling, relatable, funny and sympathetic. It’s the mark of a truly great actress.

media_title: Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die
rt_quote: Acting as a wakeup call to get off our phones and out there into the world, it’s wacky, wise and wonderfully enjoyable.
It’s hard not to be in awe of what Fastvold has achieved here. It’s a real one-off.
Fennell reflects the eventual demise of these doomed lovers with painterly melancholy. This is a disquieting and highly stylised ghost(ing) story for a new generation.
The Chronology Of Water is an intoxicating and thoughtfully crafted debut that announces Stewart as an intuitive and bold filmmaker to watch.
Though its view is unashamedly rose-tinted, Nouvelle Vague boasts a lovely lightness, a sense of the sheer thrill of doing things your own way, without fear for the consequences.
A pleasant enough film about the preservation and passing down of culture but one that seems unlikely to linger in the collective consciousness.
Park is a master of bad-taste antics and No Other Choice has bravura flourishes aplenty, including some impeccably executed death scenes.
It’s not as insightful nor quite as funny as you might hope, but it tells both sides of the story and builds compellingly to that explosive conclusion.

It’s astonishing and brave for such a mainstream franchise film to so fully embrace its more insane inclinations; DaCosta keeps things tonally on track as Alex Garland’s script boldly blends the blackest of comedy and bonkers references.
Zhao is a divinely subtle, emphatically visual filmmaker whose gift is for the deeply felt but unsaid. In her take on this love story, the most powerful moments are wordless.

Elphaba and Glinda are the gloriously compelling centre of a sometimes chortle-worthy storm. If the romance is a bit bungled, then these two fine actresses ensure that their own love story is one for the ages.
Aided by an eclectic and beautifully employed soundtrack, Ramsay gives us something that is by turns strange and haunting and bracingly real and confrontational.
A tighter edit and a touch more subtlety would have brought this horror classic more impactfully to life, but Del Toro has delivered an audacious take on a well-worn tale with bags of visual drama.
It’s a fun, fascinating and very distinct spin on the material, while the ironic, 70s-sounding title is the cherry on the cake.
A thoroughly charming, if slightly insubstantial story of good intentions and disastrous decisions.

media_title: Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery
rt_quote: The London Film Festival opening movie is a rollicking whodunnit and another slice of evidence that Josh O’Connor will soon be a household name.
While dry in its delivery, Daniel Draper’s documentary about the Women Against Pit Closures group shines a light on a piece of history fading from popular consciousness
The script is compassionate, wise and witty and the performances are exceptional.
Both explosively emotional and utterly chilling, this is phenomenal, food-for-thought filmmaking and what the expression edge-of-your-seat was made for.
The Smashing Machine is idiosyncratic and eye-catching but fails to match the power of its formidable protagonist.
It’s grand, gritty and epically long but, most of all, it’s outrageously, nay obscenely funny. Cinema really doesn’t get much more entertaining.
There’s a theatricality to the dialogue and the film’s artificiality acts as a barrier to its emotion which, given how much it wants you to buy into it, can feel frustrating.

media_title: Spinal Tap II: The End Continues
rt_quote: The classic songs, like ‘Big Bottoms’, sound as good as ever, but with no new music and nods to old gags like the Stonehenge stage set, this just feels like an ageing rock band cashing in.

Rumley (a director who has excelled at exploring the more extreme end of human nature) proves a deft hand with this difficult, morally fraught material, approaching his story with a matter-of-factness that sidesteps any dangers of sensationalism.
In its finest moments, Bulk captures the magic of talented people having a great time together and welcoming audiences along for the ride.
The whole enterprise benefits from bags of laid-back charm, a wonderful fit for a misguided yet inherently affable hero, who just cannot resist getting sucked into trouble.

Deaf takes an intimate, incisive look at the all-too common challenges of new parenthood, while presenting circumstances that are fascinatingly specific. Affecting and enlightening, it’s a powerful piece of cinema.

Outside of soap operas, teenage mothers aren’t granted much screen time, but with Young Mothers, the Dardennes take us beyond the hand-wringing headlines for a compassionate, really quite remarkable portrait of the challenges these girls face.

Chris Columbus has adapted the first of the four bestselling books in Richard Osman’s Thursday Murder Club series into a film, and it’s a frustrating affair that would have played out better as a mini-series.

media_title: Irvine Welsh: Reality Is Not Enough
rt_quote: ...this nimble, incisive and questioning documentary does a far more accurate job of articulating how Irvine Welsh deals with reality, finding fresh routes to chase oblivion, still under the chemical cosh.
It has its moments, and there’s a smattering of success in the satire. It all gets highly hysterical in the film’s final throes but by then you may be long past caring.

Dead Lover uses deliberately retro visual stylings, aggressive strobe lighting and dollar-store puppetry to create a seedy love affair that’s willing to delve into body horror and outright necrophilia.

Hysteria recognises that the immigrant experience is not one-size-fits-all, nor does Islamophobia impact everyone in the same way. That’s what makes this so engaging despite the lack of genuine suspense.
This is deeply intuitive and witty filmmaking, with a slow-burn intensity that perfectly matches the soundtrack provided by Lucy Dacus.

The film can be effervescently entertaining and its interrogatory nature is to be applauded. Frequently provocative and pretty funny, it’s a welcome injection of intelligence in a genre which has for too long been fixated on formula.
Shackleton examines our thirst for grisly murders, and, if nothing else, it’ll pique your interest in the unsolved Zodiac case.

It's the concept of a movie strung together with masking tape and baling wire. Everything about this feels like it was hastily patched together in post.
I came for the pasta, got lost in the rigatoni. Hell, yeah. I love this movie.
This film deploys visual effects and music really wonderfully.I ultimately loved it, though I have some quibbles with the pacing in the second half.
To see how they play with the comedy and the dark element of the comedy, I really liked it. It kept me interested in what was coming next.
The plot is thin, bordering on non-existent.

media_title: Ready or Not 2: Here I Come
rt_quote: It's a fun time. There are going to be a lot more deaths [than the first film]. It's a little bit longer. I felt like it kind of felt long towards the end. But, you know, there's some great needle drops.

I liked the fact that this is just about a person. And yes, she does jump into an animatronic beaver. That is true. But as a person, she's just a person. And I really, really liked Mabel as a lead character. I thought she was extremely appealing.
I appreciate how much this film is just willing to kind of go all out in the things that it's best at, instead of kind of boring us with all this connective tissue.

Nobody makes art not wanting to provoke anything. I like the fact that [Emerald Fennell] is really provoking the gut.
This movie is corny, it's gross, it's heavy handed, it lacks any subtlety whatsoever. And I absolutely loved it.
I felt like I got to know Charli XCX more than I would have with one of those kind of stage-managed Taylor Swift's many self-hagiography documentaries or any number of pop stars who have done this.
This film does a good old-fashioned favor to cinema, a huge service to cinema. Because it digs into something that's been treated so glibly by filmmakers forever, which is the question of vengeance.

I was fully wrapped up in the suspense of this. I was having a blast with the cast. And I was having a blast with the gunfights. This is blue collar entertainment as our characters are portrayed on screen.

If you can stomach the torture porn and you have seen 28 Years Later from last year, I recommend this film for the payoff that exists late in this film, which I am not going to spoil, which I found enormously enjoyable, extremely funny.
If you put this on, on a weekend afternoon, you will be fine. It is pleasant to watch. But the things that made the book special, I think, are almost impossible to preserve in a two-hour movie.

What the movie does so well is, it takes all these, like, very recognizable, like, tropey elements of this genre at this point and, like, winks at you the whole time.

media_title: Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery
rt_quote: [The film has] an incredibly rich and satisfying story, just full of kindness and compassion for the characters, and not for nothing, the very rare, really good American mainstream movie about faith, which you just don't find that many of.
There's just something very interesting about someone like George Clooney doing this sort of meta version of himself. And I think it works, in part, because George Clooney is just so charismatic.
There is almost no story here.

Jaafar Jackson & Juliano Valdi channel Michael’s spirit, but the film itself only skims the surface. The big musical numbers lean heavily on CG crowds, which end up feeling hollow rather than immersive. It feels too safe and tightly controlled.

...SO much fun and moves at 200cc. It’s super vibrant, visually stunning, and stuffed with easter eggs, but misses out on a deeper story and the chance to linger on moments that matter. Easily Illumination’s biggest and best-looking movie to date.
One of the craziest films I’ve seen in a very long time. Zazie Beetz is an absolute force of nature. Fun, freaky, and full of style.

media_title: Ready or Not 2: Here I Come
rt_quote: READY OR NOT 2: HERE I COME goes BIGGER, BADDER & BLOODIER! Radio Silence continues to raise the bar for horror-comedy with creative kills and wildly fun new characters. Samara Weaving and Kathryn Newton are a killer duo!

A THRILLING MASTERPIECE. Lord and Miller craft a BREATHTAKING SPACE EPIC filled with heart, emotion, and connection. Powered by phenomenal performances, extraordinary visuals, and scene-stealing Rocky. An unforgettable cinematic experience.
Pixar’s HOPPERS is packed with heart and absolutely hilarious. It feels like classic Pixar and is sure to be one of the funniest and fuzziest films of the year.
Wuthering Heights is a hauntingly romantic tale with a great score, strong performances, and breathtaking cinematography.
Avatar: Fire and Ash is the CINEMATIC EVENT of the year you need to see to believe and another MASSIVE visual masterpiece from James Cameron.
Marty Supreme is EUPHORIC and a straight-up a WILD RIDE. It is destined to be this year’s greatest.
ZOOTOPIA2 is FUR-ociously funny and PAWS-itively heartwarming. The Disney Animation team have delivered a wildly smart and outstanding sequel that’s well worth the wait.
Guillermo del Toro’s Frankenstein is a fresh and exhilarating take on Mary Shelley’s classic tale, featuring exceptional performances from Jacob Elordi and Oscar Isaac.
Predator: Badlands is FEROCIOUSLY FUN and surprisingly sentimental. Trachtenberg delivers a wild, relentless ride that is that is sure to be the coolest film of the year.
TRON: Ares is the COOLEST looking film of the year, with a THRILLING and completely mind-melting soundtrack from Nine Inch Nails. A visual and sonic triumph, even if a simple story holds it back.
Dwayne Johnson is terrific and gives it his all in The Smashing Machine, a visually stunning and heartfelt drama that could’ve taken even bigger swings.
A cinematic experience like no other.
TUNER is incredible. Daniel Roher plays all the right notes in a feature debut to remember. Leo Woodall & Havana Rose Liu are wonderful and work in perfect harmony.
Beautiful, heartbreaking, and brimming with soul. Joachim Trier‘s Sentimental Value is one of the very best films of the year.
Harrowing yet unexpectedly funny, It Was Just an Accident leaves a mark that stays well beyond the credits.

media_title: Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie
rt_quote: The funniest film of the decade and it’s not even close.

The Fantastic Four: First Steps is EXTRAORDINARY! The score is pure magic, the visuals are next-level, and the cast chemistry is electric. It’s bold, fresh, and unlike anything Marvel’s done before. This is their next MASTERPIECE!

SUPERMAN is a GENERATION DEFINING superhero movie and a SOARING START to the DCU. James Gunn brings heart, humility, and HOPE to the Superman movie I have been waiting my entire life for. The future of DC is very bright.
No one makes my heart ache like Celine Song. Materialists is my favourite of the year so far.
Savage and stylish, brutal and beautiful, and one of the coolest movies you’ll see this year.
Lilo & Stitch is pure Disney MAGIC and their BEST live-action reimagining yet. It’s also out of this world HILARIOUS and HEARTWARMING, with a star-making performance from Maia Kealoha.

Mission: Impossible - The Final Reckoning is a THRILLING and SHOW-STOPPING cinematic event. Tom Cruise & McQ give us EVERYTHING in this non-stop, nerve-shredding spectacle that goes deeper and darker than ever before.
THUNDERBOLTS* is Marvel at its best and a top-tier team up! Jake Schrier delivers a refreshing entry in the world of superheroes and Marvel’s most personal film yet.

Novocaine is ELECTRIFYING! A heart-racing, pulse-pounding adrenaline rush that never lets up! Jack Quaid is effortlessly charming, Amber Midthunder steals every scene & your heart. Violent and incredibly funny, it’s the PERFECT date night movie!
Messy and unsatisfying, Anthony Mackie is worthy of the shield but deserves so much better in his first big-screen outing as Cap.

A BLOOD SOAKED campy nightmare that has some of the funniest moments of the year! Mason Gooding & Olivia Holt have effortless chemistry while Gigi Zumbado brings such chaotic energy to the group! Some great moments that a sequel can refine & build on!
The Brutalist is a magnificent achievement in filmmaking, chronicling the harsh realities of the immigrant experience and the American Dream that drives it.
An unforgettable cinematic experience for one of the greatest musicals ever put to screen.
Nosferatu is Robert Eggers’ best film yet and a MASTERWORK of horror. Lily-Rose Depp and Bill Skarsgard are immaculate and deliver chilling, bloodthirsty performances.

Gladiator II is FEROCIOUSLY entertaining and the type of MYTHIC and MASSIVE filmmaking only Ridley Scott can deliver. Paul Mescal, Pedro Pascal, & Joseph Quinn are bloody glorious and bring raw charisma to every scene in this worthy sequel.
We Live In Time is completely enchanting. Andrew Garfield and Florence Pugh are a powerful pair together in a story that explores the fragility and majesty of life.

Smile 2 is a TERRIFYING MASTERPIECE! Naomi Scott delivers a blood-chilling performance that will linger in your mind for days. Parker Finn’s direction drips with dread at every turn. My heart hasn’t raced this much in years! A MUST-WATCH this Halloween!
A beautifully shot and riveting  sequel.

Transformers ONE is the BIGGEST surprise of the year and exactly the SPARK the Transformers series needed. With stunning animation, hilarious moments, and a fresh take for all fans, it’s the best Transformers movie in years.

Beetlejuice Beetlejuice is a WONDERFULLY WEIRD return to the afterlife that will leave you in stitches. Tim Burton delivers yet another must watch film for the spooky season in a sequel that is worth the wait.

Alien: Romulus is a NIGHTMARE IN SPACE! Skin-crawling perfection with BIG, EXCITING, & TERRIFYING action and sound! Fede Álvarez crafts the BEST film in the ALIEN FRANCHISE with an insane third act! Cailee Spaeny KICKS ASS. See it in IMAX.

HOLY F**K! Deadpool and Wolverine is the Marvel event of the century and the MOST FUN you’ll have at the theatre this year. Filled with heart and laughs, it’s a genuine celebration of Marvel legacy that is sure to tickle you down-under.

Twisters is the ultimate cinematic ride! Chung delivers heart-pounding thrills and epic scale that keep you on the edge of your seat! Powell & Edgar-Jones are charismatic, while the tornadoes are absolutely massive and terrifying.
Eddie Murphy brings the heat in Beverly Hills Cop: Axel F, a nostalgia-fuelled legacy sequel filled with big action, bigger laughs, and tons of heart.

Longlegs is the most TERRIFYING film of the year and will linger long after you leave the theatre. Maika Monroe is incredible and Nicolas Cage delivers a blood-curdling performance like you've never seen.

A Quiet Place: Day One is completely gripping and another incredible entry in the series. Balancing dread with moments of levity, Lupita Nyong’o and Joseph Quinn are SENSATIONAL together. We would die for Frodo the cat.
Ti West’s MaXXXine is BLOODY THRILLING and one of the best third instalments in a franchise. Mia Goth SHINES and will leave you speechless!

Inside Out 2 is ABSOLUTELY DELIGHTFUL and one of the most POWERFUL Pixar films ever made. A beautifully crafted and emotionally mature sequel that stands side by side with the original. A MUST WATCH for all ages!

Bad Boys: Ride or Die is a STYLISH, FUN, and WILDLY ENTERTAINING RIDE! Adil & Bilall deliver some of the craziest action of the series and pay tribute to all the films that came before while unfortunately putting the new story in the backseat.
Furiosa is a HEART-POUNDING adrenaline rush that DEMANDS you to WITNESS. George Miller conducts a symphony of explosions that burns rubber beginning to end and is filled with stellar performances.

media_title: Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes
rt_quote: BREATHTAKING and BEAUTIFUL. Wes Ball has laid the groundwork for the NEXT EVOLUTION of the franchise, filled with new and exciting possibilities. A true visual achievement that is sure to be one of the best films of the summer.
If you're looking for a fun, imaginative adventure with great visuals, strong voice performances, genuine heart, you should check out this movie.
Good action, great storytelling, fun characters, great moments... a crowd-pleaser.
It's so glaringly a passion project... it's momentous for Guillermo. This is fantastic.
Seeing something that is this amazing is so inspirational. It’s a hard thing to do as a filmmaker, but when it’s done right, it’s so good.
I literally could not contain myself after those first fifteen minutes. It’s impossible. It’s so funny.
Final Destination: Bloodlines just lets loose and has the best time. A very fulfilling movie-going experience.
